extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent agents and attorneys), disciplinary counsel, and attorneys advising respondents in USPTO reciprocal-discipline proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO uses to decide whether to impose reciprocal discipline (including exclusion) based on a state's disciplinary action, and the defenses a respondent must raise to avoid identical discipline under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal presumption from state disbarment (Selling standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state disbarment (or equivalent resignation in lieu) creates a federal-level presumption that imposition of reciprocal disbarment/discipline by the USPTO is proper (citing Selling v. Radford).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO follows Selling: absent one of the enumerated defenses, the Director will impose identical discipline. Federal courts and the USPTO treat the presumption as strong and require the respondent to overcome it by clear and convincing evidence. See cited cases (In re Kramer, In re Friedman, Zdravkovich, Sibley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's burden to avoid reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner bears the burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the § 11.24(d)(1) defenses (Selling elements) precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow, difficult showing. Courts have repeatedly held the respondent must produce clear and convincing evidence of a genuine issue of material fact on one of the statutory defenses; mere disagreement with the state result is insufficient (citing In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — Want of due process (§ 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will not impose identical discipline if the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must show by clear and convincing evidence that notice or hearing opportunity was constitutionally inadequate. General objections to procedure without proof of deprivation are unlikely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — Infirmity of proof (§ 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will not accept reciprocal discipline if there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to a clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the state's conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a difficult collateral-attack standard. A voluntary resignation in lieu of discipline, especially where facts are largely uncontested, ordinarily does not constitute an infirmity of proof. Courts routinely reject claims that resignation before an adjudicatory hearing shows infirmity of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — Grave injustice (§ 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal imposition of the same discipline may be defeated if the practitioner shows that doing so would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grave injustice analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct. Mere hardship to the practitioner or clients is generally insufficient; prior disciplinary history can justify harsher sanctions. Courts require clear and convincing evidence that the punishment is so ill-fitted as to be gravely unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — No public discipline in original jurisdiction (§ 11.24(d)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified in the original proceeding can be raised to oppose identical reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be supported by evidence; if the state action is effectively discipline (e.g., resignation in lieu treated as disbarment), this defense will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practitioner' and reach of reciprocal discipline (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.19, 11.24(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO regulations define 'practitioner' as 'an attorney or agent registered to practice before the Office in patent matters' and treat resignation in lieu of discipline as discipline for reciprocal-discipline purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent agents, like patent attorneys, are 'practitioners' subject to the USPTO's disciplinary jurisdiction and to reciprocal discipline when they resign in lieu or are disbarred elsewhere. Resignation in lieu may be treated as disbarment under § 11.24(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of USPTO review — not a court-of-review
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director (and courts in similar contexts) do not sit as a court of review to discover error in the state court's or hearing judge's proceedings; review is narrow and focused on the Selling elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office's inquiry is limited: it considers whether the respondent has shown a genuine issue of material fact on a Selling element by clear and convincing evidence. It will not reweigh evidence or retry the state proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timing for respondent's response to Notice and Order
rubrics_metrics.description: The Notice and Order provides the respondent a specific period (forty (40) days in this matter) to file a response opposing imposition of reciprocal discipline identical to that imposed by the other jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses must be timely filed and should raise any Selling-element defenses with supporting evidence; failure to timely respond can lead to imposition of the requested reciprocal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of sanctions the USPTO may impose identically
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless a Selling defense is proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If none of the defenses succeed, the USPTO will mirror the sanction imposed by the other jurisdiction (including exclusion from practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice obligations following discipline (§ 11.59 and Official Gazette posting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following imposition of public discipline, the OED Director must publish notice (e.g., in the Official Gazette) and give notice of the public discipline and reasons to state disciplinary agencies, courts where the practitioner is admitted, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary decisions are publicly posted (OED Reading Room) and formal notifications are required to relevant authorities per § 11.59.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of excluded practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner must comply with the duties enumerated in § 11.58 (client notification, file transfer/withdrawal, preservation of client property, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order requires compliance with § 11.58; counsel should consult § 11.58 for specific obligations (e.g., client notice, file handling, withdrawal procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/account security consequences (Customer Numbers and PKI dissociation)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO may dissociate an excluded practitioner's name from any Customer Numbers and associated public key infrastructure (PKI) certificates and prohibit the practitioner from applying for or being added to a Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order may explicitly remove access to USPTO electronic filing/customer accounts and bar future application for such access until reinstatement to practice before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to judicial review and time to seek it (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner aggrieved by the Director's action is entitled to seek judicial review on the record in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 'within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If further review is desired, the practitioner must timely file in the specified court within the statutory timeframe; counsel should follow local rules (e.g., E.D.Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law support and precedent interpreting reciprocal-discipline principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous cases hold that resignation in lieu of discipline can be treated as disbarment for reciprocal-discipline purposes and that courts will not find infirmity of proof or grave injustice absent clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases include In re Jaffe; In re Day; Attorney Grievance Comm'n v. Scroggs; In re Ngobeni; Florida Bar v. Eberhart; Disciplinary Counsel v. Acker; In re Lebowitz; In re Thav; In re Kramer. These cases illustrate the narrowness of successful defenses and are persuasive authority for the USPTO's application of § 11.24.
